topic: You miss what you are not looking for, even a gorilla
subject: psychology

sources.title: What you see is what you set: sustained inattentional blindness and the capture of awareness
How not to be Seen: The Contribution of Similarity and Selective Ignoring to Sustained Inattentional Blindness
The invisible gorilla strikes again: sustained inattentional blindness in expert observers
Gorillas in Our Midst: Sustained Inattentional Blindness for Dynamic Events
Now or never: noticing occurs early in sustained inattentional blindness
The role of perceptual and cognitive load on inattentional blindness: A systematic review and three meta-analyses

facts.claim: Eighty-three percent of radiologists did not see a gorilla that was 48 times the size of the average nodule.
facts.quote: A gorilla, 48 times the size of the average nodule, was inserted in the last case that was presented. Eighty-three percent of the radiologists did not see the gorilla.

facts.claim: The majority of radiologists who missed the gorilla looked directly at its location.
facts.quote: Eye tracking revealed that the majority of those who missed the gorilla looked directly at its location.

facts.claim: When attending to black items or white items in a dynamic display, nearly 30% of observers failed to notice a bright red cross move across the display, even though it had a unique color, luminance, shape, and motion trajectory and was visible for 5s.
facts.quote: when attending to black items or white items in a dynamic display, nearly 30% of observers failed to notice a bright red cross move across the display, even though it had a unique color, luminance, shape, and motion trajectory and was visible for 5s.

facts.claim: Doubling or even tripling the time when the unexpected object was visible barely affected the likelihood of noticing it.
facts.quote: Doubling or even tripling the time when the unexpected object was visible barely affected the likelihood of noticing it and had no impact on how accurately subjects reported its features.

facts.claim: Inattentional blindness significantly increases with the perceptual load of the task.
facts.quote: The results reveal that, in line with the perceptual account of the Load Theory, inattentional blindness significantly increases with the perceptual load of the task.

facts.claim: The most influential factor affecting noticing is a person's own attentional goals.
facts.quote: Although some stimulus properties can influence noticing of unexpected objects, the most influential factor affecting noticing is a person's own attentional goals.

research.angle: Even experts can fail to see massive, obvious objects like gorillas if their attention is focused on a specific task, regardless of whether they are looking directly at the object.
research.verdict: The evidence shows that inattentional blindness is a robust phenomenon where specific attentional goals and perceptual loads can cause people to miss highly salient, visible events.
research.caveat: The cognitive account of the Load Theory is not clearly supported by the empirical findings analyzed in the meta-analysis.
